newsitem.title: EGYPT: Jordan sees crisis unless Israel acts on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Jordan sees crisis unless Israel acts on Hebron.

text.p: Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti on Wednesday predicted a crisis if Israel failed to redeploy its soldiers in the West Bank city of Hebron.

Kabariti spoke to reporters after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on an Arab strategy toward the Israeli-Palestinian negotiations on the redeployment, widely seen as a test of the Israeli government's peace intentions.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat went in to see Mubarak shortly afterwards to brief him on the negotiations, which have made little apparent progress despite weeks of U.S. mediation. He later saw Kabariti.
"The way it looks right now is that there are differences and we hope that with the mediation of the Americans that these differences can be worked out," Kabariti said.
"I am hopeful but without the redeployment in Hebron I think that we will be having a crisis in hand," he added.
Formal talks between Israel and the Palestinians were expected to resume later on Wednesday in the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba, close to the Israeli border.
Israel, arguing that 400 Jewish settlers in the city of 100,000 Arabs need more protection, wants to renegotiate the Hebron agreement it signed with the Palestinians more than a year ago.
The Palestinians, backed by Israel's Arab neighbours, oppose any substantial changes which would dilute the powers of the Palestinian Authority.

The prime minister said Netanyahu had again told King Hussein on the telephone that Israel was committed to the 1993 agreement which laid the foundations for Palestinian autonomy in Gaza and the West Bank.

"He reiterated his commitment (to) the Oslo agreement and said he will continue working towards reaching a solution to implement it in any way that will ensure security for both the Palestinians and the Jewish population living in the Palestinian areas," he said.
"I believe there is still a chance and I hope that it won't take long for the Israeli prime minister to be convinced of the need to implement these agreements," Kabariti said.
But Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa struck a more pessimistic note, saying Israel's position was not encouraging to peace.
"It is clear that the Palestinian side does not see any progress in the negotiations and that the position now does not bode well," he told reporters after Arafat met Kabariti.

"The positions and the papers and suggestions (of Israel) cannot be considered as positive or forthcoming...they make it difficult to envisage reaching an agreement on Hebron in a short time...the position is unsatisfactory," he added.

"There is an agreement already on Hebron and this is what should be implemented and not an agreement that is parallel to it or that is a modification. Our position is unified -- we do not accept any changes to the Hebron deal and we demand that it is keenly implemented."

Palestinian officials said on Tuesday Jordan's King Hussein was trying to arrange a meeting between himself, Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to break the deadlock. But Kabariti said he knew nothing of this.
After Israeli and Palestinian negotiators worked late into Tuesday night to break the impasse over Hebron, the two sides offered sharply different views.

Arafat said talks had been fruitless, but Israeli officials dismissed his pessimism as a negotiating tactic. However, U.S. officials in Washington made clear they believed Israelis were exaggerating the progress.
